findings.paper_title: Appendix Ai - Mid-Year Treasury Management Review 2026-27
findings.headline: The council replaced £50.0m of matured PWLB short-term borrowing with shorter-term loans from other local authorities in the half year
findings.detail: The paper says the council has moved away from short-term PWLB borrowing as those loans matured, replacing them with shorter-term local authority borrowing. Local authority short-term borrowing rose to £42.0m at 30 September 2026, and the paper says the strategy exposes the council to refinancing and interest-rate risk.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can see that the council is shifting its funding toward short maturities and local authority lenders, which increases how often it must refinance.
findings.figures: £50.0m PWLB short-term borrowing matured; £42.0m local authority short-term borrowing at 30.9.26; total borrowing £51.0m at 30.9.26 against £59.0m at 31.3.26
findings.quote: as those loans have matured and has replaced them with shorter-term borrowing from other local authorities

findings.headline: East Herts retains approximately 9% of business rates collected within the district because of its tariff authority status, and the MTFP assumes business rates income growth of 2.5% per year.
findings.detail: The paper states that East Herts is a tariff authority and, once tariff payments and Section 31 grant compensation are taken into account, retains approximately 9% of the total business rates collected in the district, despite the national scheme allowing 50% growth retention. Business rates income is forecast to rise from £2,718k in 2027/28 to £2,987k in 2031/32.
findings.matters: The gap between a 50% headline growth share and the roughly 9% effectively retained is a point a finance officer at another district council or a lender would want to see stated.
findings.figures: approximately 9% of business rates collected retained; business rates income £2,718k in 2027/28 rising to £2,987k in 2031/32; 2.5% annual growth assumption
findings.quote: East Herts retains approximately 9% of the total business rates collected within the district.

findings.matters: A finance director comparing borrowing and investment rate assumptions with peers can see the spread the council is planning around, and lenders can see the rate exposure it has disclosed.

findings.headline: The 2027/28 budget includes a £128k reduction in Minimum Revenue Provision and £268k of rental income (£120k and £148k) following completion of the 2025/26 Statement of Accounts and asset review.
findings.detail: Following the 2025/26 Statement of Accounts, the council reviewed its capital financing requirement and MRP, reducing MRP by £128,000 from 2027/28. Rental income of £120,000 has been added from a commercial letting of a Council-owned asset. Rental income of £148,000 has been reinstated because the asset disposal is now expected later than previously assumed.
findings.matters: MRP changes flowing from outturn and deferred asset disposals show how capital financing and property decisions feed directly into the revenue position, a point of interest to other councils with similar asset plans.
findings.figures: MRP reduction £128k in 2027/28; rental income £120k (new letting); rental income £148k (reinstated)
findings.quote: As the disposal is now expected to occur later

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation provision of £0.5 million in each of 2026/27 and 2027/28 is retained, alongside £318,000 earmarked for workforce transition, after the Government paused implementation on 7 September 2026.
findings.detail: On 7 September 2026 the Minister for Local Government announced a review of the national LGR programme and instructed authorities to pause implementation activity. The council has nonetheless retained its LGR implementation and transition provision and its workforce transition earmark in the MTFP, as there is insufficient certainty about the review's outcome and timing to amend the assumptions.
findings.matters: Councils across England are holding LGR provisions while the programme is paused, and how each treats them in its reserves and MTFP is directly comparable.
findings.figures: £500k LGR implementation and transition provision in 2026/27 and 2027/28; £318k workforce transition / redundancy reserve in each year; total provision £818k per year
findings.quote: the Council has earmarked £318,000 in both years to support potential workforce

findings.headline: Car parking additional income target for 2027/28 is reduced from £373,000 to £273,000, with £100,000 reprofiled to 2028/29 pending the outcome of the tariff review.
findings.detail: The current MTFP assumed additional car parking income of £373,000 from 2027/28. Following the review, £100,000 has been reprofiled to 2028/29 because of uncertainty over the income that can be achieved through the ongoing tariff review. The final income may be higher or lower depending on the review outcome.
findings.matters: Parking income targets that depend on a tariff review are a common source of savings slippage, and the paper shows the target being moved rather than assumed delivered.
findings.figures: £373,000 original additional income assumption; £273,000 revised 2027/28 target; £100,000 reprofiled
findings.quote: £100,000 of this income has been reprofiled from 2027/28 to 2028/29

findings.headline: BEAM Theatre's surplus assumptions are replaced with a break-even position from 2027/28, adding a £375k pressure to the MTFP.
findings.detail: A review of BEAM's operating model and financial performance during 2026 found that the surplus assumptions in the MTFP were unlikely to be achieved in the medium term. The MTFP is now updated to assume break-even from 2027/28 onwards.
findings.matters: A council-run venue moving from an assumed surplus to break-even is a concrete example of a commercial income assumption being reset, which peers with similar venues would compare against their own.
findings.figures: £375k additional pressure in 2027/28
findings.quote: unlikely to be achieved in the medium term

findings.headline: The 2027/28 budget gap is £283k after £623k of recurring savings, with a further £1.398 million of new recurring savings to be identified across 2027/28 to 2031/32.
findings.detail: The current MTFP includes £623k of recurring savings in 2027/28, which reduces the remaining 2027/28 savings requirement to £283k. Across the five-year period, a further £1.398 million of new recurring savings will need to be identified. The Strategic Leadership Team has been tasked with developing proposals for the outstanding requirement.
findings.matters: The size and back-loading of the unidentified savings requirement is the central figure a lender or peer council would use to judge the council's medium-term budget position.
findings.figures: £283k remaining 2027/28 savings requirement; £623k recurring savings in 2027/28; £1.398 million cumulative new savings to be identified
findings.quote: Looking across the five-year planning period, a further £1.398 million of new recurring savings will need to be identified to maintain a balanced budget position.

findings.headline: The Transformation Team savings of £255k in 2027/28 are being realised earlier than the original MTFP timetable, but the full saving originally assumed will not be achieved, as two posts are retained.
findings.detail: A review completed during 2025/26 led to changes to the Transformation Team being implemented ahead of the original MTFP timetable. The review concluded that retaining two posts would provide essential capacity for digitalisation and LGR readiness, so the full saving originally assumed will not be achieved.

findings.detail: The pilot is currently running and will be monitored through the normal budget monitoring arrangements. The paper gives no income or cost figure for the pilot.

findings.headline: General fees and charges are proposed to rise by an average of 4.23% for 2027/28, adding approximately £105,200 of recurring income, of which £55,200 is new.
findings.detail: The average increase is slightly above the September 2026 CPI of 3.5%. The paper says individual charges will vary and that £50,000 of the income is already in the MTFP.
findings.matters: This is the stated average uplift on general charges against a CPI benchmark of 3.5%, which other councils can compare against their own general fee assumptions.

findings.headline: Parking tariffs in main town centre car parks are proposed to rise by up to 10 pence per hour, generating approximately £292,000 of recurring income in 2027/28, of which £20,000 is new.
findings.detail: Rural car park tariffs are proposed to stay unchanged, and the Sunday and bank holiday tariff is proposed to fall from £2.10 to £2.00. Of the £292,000, £272,000 is already in the MTFP, so the parking proposals add £20,000 towards the gap.
findings.matters: Parking is the largest single income line in the package, but most of its value is already in the budget, so the new contribution is small. The Sunday tariff reduction also moves income in the opposite direction.
findings.figures: up to 10 pence per hour; £2.10 to £2.00 Sunday and bank holiday tariff; approximately £292,000 additional recurring income; £272,000 already in MTFP; £20,000 new income

findings.headline: Garden waste subscription to rise by £3 for 2027/28, a 4.92% increase, with the garden waste income budget raised by approximately £123,000.
findings.detail: The increase is set above the general inflation assumption for fees and charges. The paper says a £30,000 rise in the income budget reflects higher resident take-up during 2026/27, and that the £3 increase is expected to generate about £93,000 of additional income.
findings.matters: It shows a council using a price rise and an observed rise in take-up together to close part of its gap, with the increase above its own inflation assumption explicitly justified.
findings.figures: £3 increase; 4.92% increase; approximately £93,000 additional income; approximately £123,000 total garden waste income budget increase; £30,000 from take-up already in MTFP
findings.quote: It is proposed to increase the garden waste subscription charge by £3 for 2027/28, equivalent to a 4.92% increase.

findings.headline: Proposed fees and charges would add £168,200 of recurring income for 2027/28 above amounts already in the MTFP, reducing the £283,000 budget gap to approximately £114,800.
findings.detail: The report totals the garden waste, parking and general fee changes at £526,200 of income, of which £352,000 is already in the MTFP. The remaining £168,200 is new income, and the paper says this would reduce the current gap. Directors are still reviewing budgets for further savings, with the outcome due in the draft budget in January.
findings.matters: A finance director or lender can see how much of a stated 2027/28 gap fee income is expected to close, and that the rest is still to be identified through budget review.
findings.figures: £283,000 budget gap; £168,200 new recurring income; £352,000 already in MTFP; £526,200 total additional income; approximately £114,800 remaining gap
findings.quote: This would reduce the current £283,000 funding gap to approximately £114,800.

findings.detail: The paper reports debt at 30.9.26 of £51.0m. The maximum debt in H1 2026/27 was £57.5m, and the paper records that borrowing complied with the authorised limit and operational boundary. The debt table also shows forecast and budget debt falling to £53.5m by 31.3.2029.

findings.headline: Financing costs are forecast at £5.743m, 26.6% of the net revenue stream, in 2026/27, up from £4.903m (23.1%) in 2025/26, and fall to £3.699m (17.2%) by 2028/29.
findings.detail: The paper sets out financing costs (interest payable and MRP charged to revenue) and their proportion of the net revenue stream for four years. The proportion rises in 2026/27 and falls in each later year shown, reaching 17.2% in the 2028/29 budget.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at another council, can compare the forecast peak and fall in financing costs as a share of net revenue with their own debt-servicing trajectory.

findings.headline: The Cyber Security risk is reviewed and held at B4, with the paper reporting significant improvements to the council's cyber security arrangements.
findings.detail: The paper says the external threat and likelihood of attempted attacks remain, so the council is continuing to focus on preventative controls and its ability to recover from an attack. It describes the improvements as significant but does not quantify them.
findings.matters: Cyber risk scores are a common benchmark in peer reviews and in lender and auditor questionnaires, and the paper states an improvement without a score change.
findings.figures: residual score B4

findings.headline: Risk 9 residual likelihood rises from 2 to 3 after the Government's LGR review, moving the residual risk from C2 to C3.
findings.detail: The paper links the change to the decision that the May 2027 elections will proceed on existing council boundaries, which it says creates uncertainty around democratic continuity. The paper says the change is a consequence of the revised LGR position.
findings.matters: A governance risk moving up a rating is a visible signal to members, auditors and peer councils about how the reorganisation pause is affecting the council's control environment.
findings.figures: residual likelihood 2 to 3; residual risk C2 to C3
findings.quote: The residual likelihood for risk 9 has consequently increased from 2 to 3

findings.headline: Risk 10 on Local Government Reorganisation moves away from the four-unitary model to cover uncertainty over structure and timetable, including potential abortive expenditure, and stays at B3.
findings.detail: Following the Government's 7 September 2026 announcement that the LGR programme would be reviewed and councils should cease implementation work, the paper says Risk 10 now focuses on uncertainty over structure and timetable. The named consequences include abortive expenditure, workforce and capacity pressures, and disruption to financial and service planning.
findings.matters: Any council that has spent money on a reorganisation programme now facing a pause or reversal needs to know how its peers are recording abortive cost and planning risk.

findings.matters: A finance director here or at a peer council can compare a stated five-year gap and a near-term 2027/28 gap against their own MTFP and see which levers the council is relying on.

findings.headline: Property fund investments wound down and capital returned in full, eliminating £12.8m exposure to illiquid pooled funds.
findings.detail: The council's two externally managed property funds completed wind-downs and returned all £12.8m of capital. Long-term treasury investments have fallen to £0.0m from £9.9m as a result. This exit complies with the 2024 CIPFA Prudential Code changes restricting local authorities from borrowing to invest for yield, and improves the treasury's liquidity position and operational flexibility.
findings.matters: Removes exposure to illiquid assets that can be difficult to access in stressed market conditions. Signals the council's compliance with restrictions on borrowing for investment purposes.
findings.figures: £12.8m returned from property funds; long-term treasury investments £0.0m (from £9.9m); part of £24.1m total investment portfolio
findings.quote: The authority was invested in two property funds, which have both wound down, with funds being returned.

findings.headline: Treasury performance generated £0.691m surplus, with investment income exceeding budget by £0.505m and interest payments running £0.186m under budget.
findings.detail: The council delivered favourable treasury outturn of £0.691m. Interest payments on borrowing totalled £3.083m against budget of £3.269m (£0.186m saving). Investment income reached £1.505m against budget of £1.000m (£0.505m above target). Strong investment income reflects active treasury management and benefits from higher short-term interest rates on cash holdings and money market fund deployments.
findings.matters: Active treasury management is delivering financial benefits that offset elements of the council's debt burden, helping to manage overall treasury costs within a higher interest rate environment.
findings.figures: Total surplus £0.691m; interest payments £3.083m vs £3.269m budget (saving £0.186m); investment income £1.505m vs £1.000m budget (surplus £0.505m)
findings.quote: The Authority produced a favourable outturn totalling £0.691m, on interest payments on Loans and interest receivable on investments.

findings.headline: Borrowing £59.0m remains £19.9m above the prudent liability benchmark of £39.1m, though gap is reducing.
findings.detail: The liability benchmark represents the lowest-risk level of borrowing needed to fund the council's capital and revenue plans while maintaining £5m minimum cash for operations. Actual borrowing at £59.0m exceeds this by £19.9m. The council acknowledges that strategies involving borrowing significantly above the benchmark carry higher risk, but reports the excess is narrowing.
findings.matters: Indicates the council is operating at higher leverage than prudent levels, with constrained financial flexibility for revenue pressures or unforeseen spending. The pathway to prudent levels requires sustained debt reduction or improved financial position.
findings.figures: Actual borrowing £59.0m; liability benchmark £39.1m; excess £19.9m; CFR £62.0m; minimum liquidity requirement £5.0m
findings.quote: The gap between the liability benchmark and existing borrowing is reducing.

findings.headline: Borrowing reduced by £5.5m to £59.0m through deployment of capital receipts during the year.
findings.detail: External debt fell from £64.5m to £59.0m as the council applied in-year capital receipts to reduce borrowing need rather than borrowing the full amount required by the General Fund Capital Financing Requirement. The CFR increased slightly from £61.8m to £62.0m, but borrowing was constrained by using available receipts.
findings.matters: Shows the council is managing to reduce leverage through capital receipts from asset sales rather than consuming cash reserves or increasing debt, which is a positive indicator of financial discipline under pressure.
findings.figures: £5.5m reduction; borrowing fell from £64.5m to £59.0m; CFR £62.0m (up £0.2m)
findings.quote: Short-term borrowing reduced, as in year capital receipts were used to offset borrowing.

findings.headline: Short-term borrowing represents 97.46% of the council's £59.0m external debt, with new long-term borrowing deferred as PWLB rates remain high at 5.72% for 10-year loans.
findings.detail: The council has paused new long-term borrowing and is managing the debt portfolio using short-term facilities. £50m is borrowed from PWLB short-term at an average rate of 4.85%, with £7.5m from other local authorities at 4.35%, all repayable within 12 months. The 10-year PWLB rate ended the year at 5.72%, compared to 5.38% at the start. This strategy concentrates refinancing risk if rates remain elevated or if short-term funding becomes constrained.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council faces identical pressure on long-term borrowing costs and needs to understand how peers are managing refinancing risk. A lender needs to assess whether the council can reliably refinance £57.5m of maturing debt each year.
findings.figures: £59.0m total borrowing; 97.46% under 12 months; £50m PWLB short-term at 4.85%; £7.5m from other local authorities at 4.35%; 10-year PWLB rate 5.72% (started 5.38%)
findings.quote: The Authority's short-term borrowing has continued, as entering into any longer-term debt is on hold, due to long term PWLB interest rates remaining high.

findings.headline: General Fund balances assessed as adequate but earmarked reserves under review to identify resources for redeployment to support medium-term sustainability
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer has determined that General Fund balances remain adequate to support financial resilience, with a minimum level calculated at £3.578 million for 2027/28 based on risk factors including service demand volatility, inflationary pressures, commercial income uncertainty and Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty. However, the council is undertaking a comprehensive review of earmarked reserves to ensure they remain appropriately aligned to strategic priorities and financial risks, and to identify whether resources can be released to support medium-term financial sustainability. The outcome will be reported as part of the draft budget in January 2027.
findings.matters: Whilst balances are currently adequate, the potential release of earmarked reserves suggests the council may need to redeploy funds to address the medium-term budget gap, indicating tightening financial headroom.
findings.figures: Minimum General Fund balance: £3.578 million for 2027/28; Gross Revenue Expenditure 3% = £2.927m, Annual Gross Capital Expenditure 4% = £0.085m, Council Tax adjustment 4% = £0.566m
findings.quote: A review of earmarked reserves is currently being undertaken to ensure that reserves remain appropriately aligned to the Council's strategic priorities, financial risks and emerging commitments, including preparations for Local Government Reorganisation.

findings.headline: Council holds approximately £50 million borrowing with 4.5% annual cost assumptions throughout planning period
findings.detail: The MTFP notes that the council has approximately £50 million of borrowing outstanding. The financial plan assumes borrowing costs of 4.5% annually, based on current Public Works Loan Board rates and market forecasts, described as prudent assumptions. Given the scale of the borrowing, changes in interest rates could have a significant material impact on the council's financing costs and overall financial position.
findings.matters: A substantial borrowing book means interest rate movements could materially improve or worsen the financial position; if rates fall, the position improves, but they are assumed to remain elevated at 4.5%.
findings.figures: Council borrowing: approximately £50 million; assumed borrowing interest rate: 4.5% throughout planning period
findings.quote: With approximately £50 million of borrowing, changes in Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) and wider market interest rates can have a significant impact on financing costs and the Council's overall financial position.

findings.headline: 2027/28 savings programme of £623,000 identified; only £130,000 of further savings proposed for 2028/29, leaving later years without defined solutions
findings.detail: The council has identified £623,000 of recurring savings for 2027/28, comprising civil parking enforcement (£273,000), transformation team restructure (£255,000), ground maintenance re-procurement (£50,000), garden waste charges (£30,000), and EV charger income (£15,000). For 2028/29, only £130,000 of savings are currently identified. The council has also deferred £100,000 of previously anticipated car parking income from 2027/28 to 2028/29, reflecting uncertainty about achievable income levels from tariff reviews.
findings.matters: The concentration of identified savings in year one, with minimal savings identified for subsequent years, indicates that most of the remaining gap (years 2-5 totalling £1.398 million cumulative) currently lacks defined solutions.
findings.figures: 2027/28 recurring savings £623,000 (civil parking £273k, transformation £255k, maintenance £50k, waste £30k, EV £15k); 2028/29 savings £130,000; car parking income reprofiled: £100,000 deferred
findings.quote: The current MTFP includes £623k of recurring savings in 2027/28, reducing the remaining savings requirement for that year to £283k

findings.headline: Council retains £818,000 annual provision for Local Government Reorganisation costs despite government pause on the programme
findings.detail: Although the government announced on 7 September 2026 that it was pausing Local Government Reorganisation implementation activity pending a review of the national programme, East Hertfordshire has retained financial provisions totalling £818,000 annually (£500,000 for implementation and transition costs, £318,000 for potential workforce transition and redundancy costs) in both 2026/27 and 2027/28. The council considers these provisions prudent given the uncertainty around the outcome and timetable of the government review.
findings.matters: The council is maintaining material contingency provisions for an uncertain event; if reorganisation is significantly delayed or abandoned, these could be released; if accelerated, they may prove insufficient.

Interest payments on loans came in £0.186m under budget at £3.083m actual v £3.269m budgeted. However, with Bank Rate now at 3.75% and held stable per MPC guidance, and Arlingclose forecasting rates to remain at 3.75%, the elevated investment returns achieved during the year (when rates were higher) are unlikely to recur.
findings.matters: A lender would note that the favorable treasury surplus appears driven by timing of high interest rates during the year, not sustainable income generation. Council budgets may need revision if investment income declines materially in 2026/27.
findings.figures: Treasury surplus £0.691m; Interest payments: budget £3.269m, actual £3.083m, favorable variance £0.186m; Investment income: budget £1.000m, actual £1.505m, favorable variance £0.505m
findings.quote: The Authority produced a favourable outturn totalling £0.691m, on interest payments on Loans and interest receivable on investments.

findings.headline: Council holds £12.3m in commercial and property investments purchased for yield and is divesting before taking new borrowing.
findings.detail: The council holds £4.3m of commercial investments plus £8m being marketed for sale, purchased before CIPFA Prudential Code changes prohibited borrowing to invest primarily for financial return. The council has explicitly stated it will review exit options 'before undertaking further additional borrowing'. Two property funds have already wound down, returning £9.9m. Non-treasury subsidiary investments of £5.0m (shareholdings £1.7m, loans £3.3m) generated only 2.8% return (£0.143m income).
findings.matters: A lender would see this as the council realigning away from leveraged investment strategies and back towards alignment with current prudential code. Successful divestment of these assets could materially improve the council's net borrowing position.
findings.figures: Commercial investments held £4.3m, being marketed £8.0m; Property funds wound down £9.9m; Non-treasury subsidiary investments £5.0m at 2.8% return
findings.quote: The Authority currently holds £4.3m in commercial investments plus a further £8m currently being marketed for sale that were primarily purchased for financial return prior to the change in the CIPFA Prudential Code.

findings.headline: Borrowing of £59.0m exceeds the prudent liability benchmark of £39.1m by £19.9m; long-term borrowing is on hold pending rate improvement.
findings.detail: The council's external borrowing sits £19.9m above the liability benchmark (which estimates minimum borrowing needed to fund planned capex while maintaining £5m minimum liquidity). The council has explicitly paused long-term borrowing due to high PWLB rates: 10-year maturity rose from 5.38% at April 2025 to 5.72% at year-end, well above Bank Rate of 3.75%. The council expects future rate reductions. The gap between borrowing and benchmark has narrowed from £31.8m (2025) to £19.9m (2026).
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about borrowing above prudent levels, though the narrowing trend suggests improving discipline. The rate environment is also material—frozen long-term borrowing could indicate either prudent timing or deferred capital spending.
findings.figures: Liability benchmark £39.1m; Actual borrowing £59.0m; Gap £19.9m (vs £31.8m prior year); 10-year PWLB rate: 1 April 5.38% → 31 March 5.72%; Bank Rate: 4.50% → 3.75%
findings.quote: The Authority's short-term borrowing has continued, as entering into any longer-term debt is on hold, due to long term PWLB interest rates remaining high.

findings.headline: 97.46% of the £59.0m borrowing portfolio matures within 12 months, concentrated in £50m of short-term PWLB loans.
findings.detail: The council's debt is heavily skewed to short-term maturity with only £1.5m long-term fixed borrowing (8.875%, 29-year maturity). The £50m of short-term PWLB loans carry a 4.85% average rate and will be replaced with inter-local authority borrowing on maturity. This concentration exposes the council to material refinancing risk if capital markets deteriorate or short-term rates spike when these loans are rolled over.
findings.matters: A lender would assess refinancing risk; if short-term rates rise materially, the council's cost of borrowing could increase significantly at point of maturity. The reliance on inter-local authority lending for renewal also creates counterparty concentration risk.
findings.figures: Maturity structure: under 12 months 97.46%, 10+ years 2.54%; Short-term PWLB £50m at 4.85% average; Long-term PWLB £1.5m at 8.875%
findings.quote: The average rate on the Authority's short-term PWLB loans of £50m, as at 31st March 2026 was 4.85%, these will be replaced with inter local authority borrowing on maturity.

findings.headline: Net borrowing increased from £30.4m to £34.9m as investment balances fell by £10.0m.
findings.detail: Despite external borrowing falling by £5.5m (used capital receipts for repayment), net borrowing position worsened by £4.5m because total investment balances fell sharply from £34.1m to £24.1m. Long-term treasury investments were eliminated entirely (from £9.9m to nil) following wind-down of two property funds. The council is consuming resources faster than reducing debt, indicating worsening underlying financial position.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council is drawing down its cash reserves even while reducing gross borrowing, suggesting it may be in structural deficit and could require additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Net borrowing: 31.3.25 £30.4m → 31.3.26 £34.9m (increase £4.5m); Total investments: £34.1m → £24.1m (decrease £10.0m); Long-term investments: £9.9m → £0
findings.quote: Short-term borrowing reduced, as in year capital receipts were used to offset borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Update on Assets of Community Value
findings.headline: New Sporting ACV regime could indefinitely restrict hundreds of council sports facilities, with unclear listing criteria and guidance pending.
findings.detail: The new legislation introduces Sporting ACVs with indefinite listing (versus ten years for standard ACVs). The district has over 500 sports facilities: 184 football pitches, 53 rugby pitches, 46 cricket pitches, 135 tennis courts, 81 netball pitches, and 13 lawn bowls greens. These could all face disposal restrictions and compensation claims. The council acknowledges uncertainty about how listings will be decided and notes the need for clarity before implementation.
findings.matters: Asset restrictions affecting council-owned facilities constrain management flexibility and create potential liabilities. Lenders assess a council's ability to monetise or dispose of assets; indefinite restrictions on hundreds of facilities materially affect that capacity.
findings.figures: 184 football pitches, 53 rugby union pitches, 46 cricket pitches, 135 tennis and padel courts, 81 netball pitches, 13 lawn bowls greens
findings.quote: The Playing Pitch and Outdoor Sports Strategy which was adopted by Executive in November 2025 as part of the evidence base for the review of the District Plan identified East Herts has, by way of example: - 184 football pitches - 53 rugby union pitches - 46 cricket pitches - 135 tennis and padel courts - 81 netball pitches - 13 lawn bowls greens

findings.paper_title: Update on Assets of Community Value
findings.headline: New legislation requires independent valuations for community property purchases, but the council does not know who will pay for them.
findings.detail: The 2026 Act introduces a Community Right to Buy for ACVs, with purchase price set by independent valuation at open market value. The paper explicitly states that guidance is awaited on who will undertake these valuations and whether the council will bear the cost. This creates an unquantified future cost exposure with no identified budget provision.
findings.matters: Unquantified and unbudgeted costs represent a balance sheet and cash flow risk. A finance director cannot forecast expenditure without knowing whether and when these costs will materialise.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: it is not clear who will be responsible for undertaking independent valuations (2.17) and whether this cost will fall on the Council.

findings.paper_title: Update on Assets of Community Value
findings.headline: Landowners can claim compensation for losses caused by ACV listing, creating an acknowledged but unquantified contingent liability.
findings.detail: The council recognises that property owners can claim compensation for revenue losses resulting from ACV listing, if loss is proved on the balance of probabilities. East Herts has received no such claims to date. However, the paper does not quantify potential exposure, establish any reserve, or set parameters for what constitutes recoverable loss.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors require visibility of contingent liabilities. An undefined but acknowledged exposure affects the council's risk profile and may require provisioning.
findings.figures: Zero claims received to date
findings.quote: it is possible that where a landowner has lost revenue as a result of an ACV listing (eg. it prevented or led to a loss of a sale) they can claim compensation. The loss would need to be proved on the balance of probabilities. To date East Herts have not received any claims.

findings.headline: £237k of capital spending will not be delivered in 2026/27: URC Church Hall (£170k) and ORL Town centre regeneration (£67k) are carried forward to 2027/28

findings.matters: Capital programme slippage of this scale (10% of the revised budget) signals delivery challenges, affects treasury planning and cash flow, and impacts the council's ability to deliver planned services and infrastructure investment.

The build-back work is substantial and must be undertaken alongside the 2025/26 and 2026/27 audits to meet the statutory backstop date.
findings.matters: If the audit cannot be completed by the deadline, the council remains without an unqualified audit opinion, prolonging the period of financial statement assurance gaps that concern lenders.

The council explicitly states this additional cost will create pressure on its revenue budget, likely split across 2026/27 and 2027/28.
findings.matters: A £245k unbudgeted expense represents a material revenue pressure on the council's finances, directly resulting from its failure to maintain adequate audit trail and account balances in prior years.

findings.headline: Council received disclaimed audit opinions for four consecutive years (2021/22 to 2024/25)
findings.detail: East Hertfordshire has not received an unqualified audit opinion for four years. A disclaimed opinion is the most serious audit outcome, indicating the auditor could not form an opinion on whether the financial statements are fairly presented. The current audit plan includes a specific Build-back Plan to rebuild assurance on the council's account balances.
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion signals that the council's financial statements cannot be relied upon, which is fundamental information for lenders assessing creditworthiness and for the finance director managing the council's finances.
findings.quote: The Council has received a disclaimed audit opinion for the years 2021/22 to 2024/25, the audit will present the Build-back plan (as attached at Appendix B). This sets out the proposed approach by the auditors to build back assurance on the Councils balances.

findings.headline: Liquid investment balances fell 29% as the council depleted reserves to reduce debt
findings.detail: Balance sheet resources (the council's investment/cash balances) fell from £34.1m to £24.1m, a £10m reduction. Capital receipts were used to pay down short-term borrowing rather than rebuild reserves. While the property fund return of £12.8m was planned and positive, the net effect is a significantly depleted cash cushion.
findings.matters: At the same time as the council is concentrating refinancing risk (97% of debt under 12 months) and deferring long-term borrowing on a bet that rates fall, it is also reducing its financial buffers. If capital receipts dry up or unexpected pressures arise, the council has less liquidity to absorb shocks without new borrowing.

The authority explicitly states it will not undertake further borrowing until these are exited.
findings.matters: These legacy investments are a constraint on future capital flexibility. Until they are sold, they prevent the council from using standard borrowing instruments and tie up capital that could otherwise service debt. Sale delays or shortfalls could force difficult choices.

findings.headline: Long-term borrowing deferred while betting PWLB rates will fall below 5.72%

The treasury strategy states 'entering into any longer-term debt is on hold, due to long term PWLB interest rates remaining high.' This is a bet that rates will fall before the council needs to lock in long-term debt.
findings.matters: If PWLB rates stay elevated or rise, this leaves the council forced to keep refinancing at short-term rates (currently 5-7%), with no option to lock in. Every year the council waits, the risk of having to accept higher long-term rates increases.

findings.headline: Nearly all borrowing (97%) matures within 12 months, creating annual refinancing risk

This forces the council to refinance almost its entire borrowing annually. At year-end, short-term rates spiked to 5-7%, up from 4-4.5% earlier.
findings.matters: This maturity profile exposes the council to refinancing risk: if rates remain elevated or tighten further, rolling over £57m of maturing debt annually could blow the budget. There is no certainty costs will be stable.
findings.figures: £57.5m short-term borrowing (97.46% of total), short-term rates 5.0%-7.0% at year-end vs 4.0%-4.5% earlier, 4-month weighted average maturity
